utterances.text: This is an update to a situation report from UNMO headquarter BH command in Sarajevo -- to UNMO headquarter BH Command Sarajevo from UNMO headquarter BH Sector North-East. If you can look at the DTG, that is the date time group, this was on 8th at 1430 hours in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that B that follows the time of 1430, what does that stand for, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: B, that is Bravo, is a time zone and we have a several time zones in the world. We have Zulu, Bravo, and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you said -- you referred to BH Sector North-East. That was based in Tuzla, is that correct, just so there is no doubt about what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look in paragraph 1, there's a reference to the BiH Chief of Staff, and I think that's abbreviated as COS. Do you see where it says: "The BiH COS has informed UNMOs that over 100 shells have landed." That's almost in the middle of paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Let me look for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we move a little bit to the right side so that we see the first letter of each line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, can I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So this report contains this line that the BiH Chief of Staff has informed UNMOs that over 100 shells have landed in the general area of Bleceva [phoen] and Cimzic [phoen]. But this is," and then's an abbreviation and this is what I wanted to ask you about. It is written here: "But this is NCBU." What does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be enlarged a little bit more, as we had it before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, NCBU --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: NCBU, to us, meant "not confirmed by UNMOs." In this case, what we mean is, as military observers, we were sending reports indicating what we have observed, but something that comes to us from another source, we had to indicate to the headquarter that we personally have not confirmed it. But in the process would go out there and confirm and then report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to the very end of the paragraph, it says "Note," and this is at the end of paragraph 1: "Note, use this as our DSR if we do not send it on time, as we are now heading for the bunker." Can you just tell us, please, what DSR means?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, DSR means "daily situation report." This is what we sent, you know, sending every day in the evening, but in the course of the day, if something arises, we used to send updates like this one. But due to constraints, we had to indicate here that if we are unable to send a daily situation report, they can use the update that we have given as the normal DSR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the very bottom of the document, at the sign-off it says: "Regards Team Srebrenica (through HQ Sector North-East)." Can you just explain what that means, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: You can see up there, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Previous page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If can you see the indication where we have a "To," is to UNMO headquarter BH Command Sarajevo and UNMO headquarter Zagreb. That is where the destination of this update was. But because of communication problems, sometimes you cannot get through immediately, so we had to go through headquarters Sector North-East so that they can retransmit the same to these other destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we're done with that exhibit. Thank you very much. I wanted to ask you about one topic you testified about, and this was at transcript page 19441 to 19442 of your Popovic testimony, just for the record. There, you testified about the VRS shelling of the Srebrenica town, and you used the word "crushed" to describe how they were crushed into a particular area. Can you just describe for the Trial Chamber in a little bit more detail what you meant by that. What were you explaining in Popovic when you talked about the civilians being crushed into an area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this is P950.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I mean -- what I meant by this was that these people were being forced into a certain direction, in that the shelling was sort of patterned to force the people to flee towards a certain direction, and what this means is that they had no choice other than to go directly to the direction that they're being forced to. There were no alternatives. So they had to go directly towards -- those from [indiscernible] and other outlying villages had to go towards Srebrenica itself. And after that, they were forced now to flee towards a safer place which was the DutchBat compound. So this what I meant by "crushing." They were being forced into one direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "DutchBat compound," sir, where was that compound located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, DutchBat compound, this is the compound that belonged to the battalion of Netherlands, and it was located in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the next couple of minutes, I'd like to show you some very brief video-clips and just ask you a couple of questions about them. This is from the Popovic trial video P991. And it is subtitled, so the interpreters can take a break and we can just watch the movie for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, we're starting at 1 hour, 58 minutes, and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've stopped the video at 1 hour, 58 minutes, 34.4 seconds. First of all, can you identify yourself anywhere in this video. And if you could just briefly explain the location, and if you recall the date.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Sir, I can see myself behind there somewhere, but some of these person look slightly younger than I am now. I'm the one behind there. And this happened outside the DutchBat compound but slightly towards Srebrenica village where the -- the IDPs or refugees, whatever you may call them, were located. I hope you still remember that we had two areas where these refugees were located. One of them was inside the DutchBat compound, both inside the warehouses and outside, and also in a factory located just about 3, 3 or 400 metres from the DutchBat compound as you go towards Srebrenica town. So as can you see, here we have General Ratko Mladic and other officers from the BSA side, and DutchBat officers. We were trying to discuss with them on what should be done now that the situation has really changed. But it was very difficult because of a communication barrier, and for me, I had to look for officers who could be able to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, just for the record, can you describe the colour of the vest that you're wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The colour, Your Honours, as can you see, is blue, and the helmet is also blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another clip very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, we're at 2 hours, 27 minutes of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've stopped at 2 hours, 28 minutes, 45.7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, Colonel, please, what was going on in this footage that we just saw. What are you talking, and what brought you to this location, and who are you speaking to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was one of the most trying moments in my stay in Srebrenica, in that we had no water and we had to request water to be brought, and luckily, the BSA agreed to bring water for the people. After that, I had to look for people who could be able to speak English because I had really noticed that men had been separated from women and children by the BSA and had been taken to -- had been taken to one of the houses, specifically a white house, where, according to my assessment, they were overcrowded. They were sitting on each other. There was no proper aeration, no proper sanitation facilities. And they were huddled there, not being assisted, you know, in anything. So this had really annoyed me a bit, in that I had to look for BSA officer who could be able to go there and assist. Unfortunately, most of them could not speak English and I had to identify some who could be able to convey the message to their senior officers. That is, including the colonels who were there. We're talking about Colonel Vukovic, Colonel Drcic, General Ratko Mladic, and all those senior officers who there were, so that could be done about the civilian -- the -- the men who were huddled in one particular house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one more clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are at 2 hours, 29 minutes, 20 seconds of the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether you will be would be able to go back a bit. If you are able to go back a bit, where you have started, because there's some items which are located somewhere. And if you allow me, I can talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again we're back at 2 hours, 29 minutes and 22.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Go ahead, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the men were being separated from the women and children, they were taken to a white house, as I have said earlier. They were forced to leave their belongings on the way, somewhere on the road before they entered the house, and these are some of their belongings. Here we are talking about -- they had luggage that they had or the documents, including identification cards, wallets, that includes even money. Anything that they had, they had to drop it here before entering the -- that white house. So these are some of the belongings that belonged to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the documents that were among the items that the men who were in the white house were forced to leave there in the pile. Did that cause any concern for you, Colonel, that documents were being left in the pile, that these men were forced to leave their documents outside this white house before going in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, to me it meant a lot, and I mentioned it somewhere during cross-examination here sometime back. And it meant that these people, whatever is going to be done to them, it would be very difficult to identify them later, because all the identification documents have been left somewhere. And if really you don't have any bad intention, you don't take documentation from people. You let them have their documentation so that you can easily identify who this particular person is. But this was an indicator that something bad was going to happen, and we mentioned in our reports to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just continue the video for another minute or so, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we've stopped at 2 hours, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, please, tell the Trial Chamber what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, here, we are discussing with BSA officers. The one in a blue flak-jacket is one of those I had identified that could speak English and he was assisting us in translation, because I was talking to that senior officer next there and I had to be -- let them know that what they have done is really wrong. This is in terms of putting people in one place, removing their documentation, and also not being seen to mind about their welfare, as earlier discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, this still has four men in it, two of whom are wearing blue berets. The senior officer that you were just referring to, is that the third individual from the left who is wearing a white T-shirt underneath his camouflage uniform? Is that who you are talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's true. This is the one who is third from the left, my left, and wearing a white T-shirt inside. The other officer that can you see on the extreme left is also a BSA officer but wearing a blue UN beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's continue rolling the video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Did I understand you correctly, this is in -- an officer of the BSA wearing a blue beret of the UN forces. Is that true? And what might be the explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true, sir. Upon -- just before the fall of the enclave, they had surrounded several observation posts, in short, OPs, which were being manned by the Dutch battalion and they had taken everything, including their clothing. Some even came back naked. They also took even their armoured personnel carriers, and they wanted to sort of disguise like they are UN personnel, whereas they were not, so that they could be able to access without being known to be BSA officers. So this to us was -- at least we had seen that before. And also the one who was to the right, the one who could speak English, you can see he has a blue flak-jacket and this was actually UN property stolen by these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another question by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to follow up on the question from the Presiding Judge. The blue beret from the UN that is wearing the officer [as interpreted] in question, I was wondering whether it was bearing the insignia of the UN or whether it was just blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it had that insignia. But in most cases they were not removing it. They were wearing it with the insignia on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could continue rolling the video for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've stopped at 2 hours, 30 minutes, 46.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell the Trial Chamber what's depicted in this video still. We see a balcony of a building with a number of men seated close together on it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the balcony of the house -- of the white house that I talked about. This is where the -- the men who were separated from their families were kept. Some were up there in the balcony, others were down there in the ground floor. And these were very many men in a very small area. And that is why I really complained about it. There were very many -- as can you see, there's no breathing space. And these ones are better because at least they are in the upper floor. But the ones who are down there were really suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with this exhibit. Just a couple of more questions for you, Colonel. I want to show you a very brief excerpt from some video footage that we did not have in our possession at the time you testified in 2007 and 2008. This has, I believe, already been shown to the Trial Chamber, but I just want to show some excerpts from it and see if you can identify yourself and explain what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is from V000-8122, which is P236, P00236. We're starting at 2 hours, 18 minutes, 1.5 seconds of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've stopped at 2 hours, 18 minutes and 21 seconds. Please tell the Trial Chamber what's going on here. If you can remember what day this was. And do you see yourself anywhere in this frame. If you do, can you just describe what you're wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see myself there in a blue flak-jacket and a blue helmet, and picking up bread from the lorry that had brought it. What we're doing here is to distribute the bread which had been brought by the BSA to the IDPs who were huddled outside the factory that I alluded to earlier and who were very hungry and very thirsty at that particular moment. So the bread came straight away, after the water had been brought, and we decided to assist in distributing the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we're done with this exhibit. Now, finally, sir, I just wanted to ask you a couple of questions that didn't come up in the Popovic trial. It's in your OTP statement, and you do talk about the general topic in the Popovic case. At transcript page, for the record, 19279, you testified that after the civilian population had been removed from Potocari one of the major issues became what to do with the sick, injured and wounded who remained on the Potocari UN compound, as well as what to do with the Muslim civilian employees of DutchBat and the other NGOs. And you then testified at transcript page 19824 to 19825 about efforts that were made to transport those sick and wounded from Potocari to Bratunac. In connection with those efforts, do you recall any lists being made, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a list that was made, but this was to enable us know who the injured and the sick were. The list was made by both us and the MSF, mainly by the MSF, but we did it together because they were the ones who knew those who were sick and what was ailing them. If it was injuries, they could indicate what was actually wrong with them. But we did it together. So this was to enable us evacuate the same people, that is, the injured and the sick, so that they can get treatment, you know, better treatment so that can get cured. The other reason was to make sure that at least we know who is where and especially concerning the -- the injured. We had Mr. -- Major Nikolic going around and checking those who are in the hospital -- in the DutchBat compound, whether they -- they were part of the -- the soldiers -- the Muslim soldiers, and so we wanted to make sure that at least we have a proper list that we can use. Now, on the interpreters. I thought you asked about the interpreters also.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any lists that you recall being made with respect to the interpreters and the other civilian employees of the NGOs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had to make a list of interpreters and the other employees of NGOs because we wanted to make sure that they get a good exit out of the enclave in a safe way. We wanted to make sure that we were given permission to leave the enclave together so that their lives are not endangered. If they could have been left in the enclave, definitely something bad could have happened to them, and so we actually wanted to be evacuated together with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the list of the wounded, you referred to Major Nikolic going around and checking those people, can you first just tell the Trial Chamber who -- who Major Nikolic was, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was Major Nikolic was the main link between us and the BSA. To us, he was a local commander in that particular area, and he could meet us once a week, or when situation required that we meet. We could request to meet him and he could also request to meet us in case of anything. This was being done through an interpreter who was called Mr. Peter and who had our own UN communication equipment. He had a radio that we could be able to call him through and convey a message to Major Nikolic and vice versa. Some of these meetings were to convey some messages and especially if something had happened from the BSA side that Major Nikolic or the BSA wanted the Muslims to know about. Or, serious meetings like when Colonel Vukovic wanted to meet us, he conveyed the message through Major Nikolic to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned safety concerns for the interpreters, for example, and that was one of the reasons why you made the list of the interpreters. To what degree did similar concerns play in the decision to make the list of the wounded, which included possible military-aged men? In other words, did you have the same concerns for some of the wounded that you listed that you had for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, even in war, the injured are given a human face. They're supposed to be treated. They're supposed to face the same situation as the friendly forces, not as enemy forces. Because they are no longer active in war. That is, even if they were fighting soldiers, they are no longer active. So according to the Geneva Convention, they're supposed to be treated in a humane way. And that is what caused concern to us, in that even if they are injured, they've got to be evacuated and treated in a good hospital so that they can recover. So that is why we had to make that list, to make sure that those are also evacuated from that particular enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, did everybody that were -- who was on these two lists make it out safely in the end?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I'm concerned, I think those who were in that list made it safely outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last thing I'd like to do is -- and this is with the Court's permission. There are two documents which I identified after we had issued the list that hadn't been used in the Popovic case. I notified the Defence that if there were -- there was no objection and the foundation were laid by Colonel Kingori, that we might seek to tender these with the Court's permission. They do not have 65 ter numbers. They were not part of the 92 bis package. They were, however, part of the original OTP witness statement that everybody's had for years. They were part of the same package that included all the sitreps, most of which the Trial Chamber has before it. What I'd like to do is be able to show these to the witness just to lay the foundation for their authenticity, and if the Court requires, I can make it part of a formal motion to add these two documents to the 65 ter list later, or if there's no objection and the Court deems it appropriate, we can do that now and simply add them now. I think they're uploaded. We have temporary -- or 65 ter numbers assigned to them and it's just a matter of showing them to the witness so he can identify them for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't know which other document it concerns because we don't have that document. Maybe the Prosecution can indicate the number. It's difficult to proceed with cross-examination today without knowing which document is in question. We know about one document; we don't know about the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber is in the same position as you. Perhaps, Mr. Thayer, you can be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I made sure that the Defence had hard copies of the documents. Mr. Gajic has them. I've identified them by ERN, and location and page, both in English and B/C/S for the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You might just give an indication of which documents you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're referring to 65 ter 6540 and 6541. There might be some confusion. I think the packet I gave to the Defence may have been stapled as one document and that might be the confusion as to whether there's one document or two documents. But it is in fact two lists that were part of the witness's OTP statement. So we can put them up on the ELMO. They are uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we'll see that -- if Mr. Gajic is looking at the packet I gave him, the first document ends at 00527591, and then the other one picks up at 7592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I saw you were on your feet. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All the documents are put together in one file which bears one number, and we will look into it before cross-examination. But we would appreciate it if the Prosecution could separate these documents because they are, by their nature, separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are uploaded in e-court, both of them, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: They, are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we would like to see them. You can clarify if it's one document or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly. May we see 6540, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told, are they released to the Chamber -- to the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We thought so, Mr. President. If -- I'm -- I'm getting confirmation that they are. If they are slow to come up or if they are in the ether somewhere, I've got hard copies we can place on the ELMO without a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And on both sides, we see the same document. Perhaps we need only one. Could be enlarged a bit. Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise what this document is before you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Sir, this is the document that I talked about, that is, the list of the injured who were in DutchBat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in the upper left-hand corner, we see somebody has written "Attachment number 20, page 1." That was done by Mr. Ruez, the OTP investigator who interviewed you in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And over on the right there appears to be a signature. Do you know whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Definitely sir. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 8 of this document, please. And just scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see there were 60 names typed and then there are three additional names that were added by hand. Who added those names, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm the one who added these names for these three other people. And, as you can see, what I've written down there, they are family members of some of the wounded persons that would have wanted to be evacuated together with the injured and the sick from the enclave. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One observation, we see a typed list with 60 names. Then the number 61 is missing, and then we have three numbers, handwritten 61 -- sorry, 62, 63 and 64. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we see 65 ter 6541, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the list of interpreters, that is, both for DutchBat and slightly there you can see those for UNMO interpreters, and below that, the refugee representatives in the enclave. So this is the list that we prepared together with the earlier list so that we could get a safe exit from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can just scroll to the top of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see in the upper left-hand corner what's written: "Attachment number 21, page 1." And, again, on the right-hand corner, can you identify the signature there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is, too, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down to the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In addition to the refugee representatives you just spoke about there's also somebody who is listed as an MSF female personnel. And if we can go to the next page, we can also see individuals who were being identified from UNHCR and again from MSF. Sir, did Mr. Ruez have these documents already when he met with you, or did you have them with you and you gave them to him during your interview?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are documents that I had with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In other words, you brought them out of the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I'm saying, that these are some of the documents I managed to get out of the enclave with and I went with them to Kenya, including even some of the situation reports which were not initially part of the UN system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter numbers 6540, 6541, unless there's an objection, or if the Defence needs some time to review, I certainly will understand the -- a delay in doing that. But I would tender them at this point. JUDGE FLUEGGE. If I understood you correctly, you are moving for addition to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do not object, but this should be admitted as one document, not two. We don't want to speculate. We never have, and we never will, until the end of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand the Prosecution that these are in fact two documents. That's two different 65 ter numbers. And after having heard the explanation of the witness, in fact, they are two different lists. One containing 63 names, and the other without any numbering of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the -- your motion will be granted. The documents will be entered to the 65 ter exhibit list and both documents will be received as exhibits. But, let me tell you the opinion of the Trial Chamber. It's really a last-moment application, and we would be very glad if you could deal with these problems a little earlier for the sake of the proceedings of the Chamber and for the preparation of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is, indeed, Mr. President. I apologise again. I only realised this yesterday, unfortunately. And as soon as I did, I communicated all this information to the Defence. And again, I apologise, and I thank the Court for its flexibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 6540 will be Exhibit P1002. 65 ter 6541 will be Exhibit P1003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. And I thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome the witness and I wish him a pleasant stay in our midst, and I would invite him to answer according to his conscience. Please, sir, Mr. Kingori, could you please tell us, before you arrived in the territory of Yugoslavia, did you undergo a special training, special education, to teach you about the history of the conflict in the area where you were being sent as a -- an observer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Sir, maybe before I answer the question I will request that I see what is being said on the -- because I cannot see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have some help from the court assistants with the LiveNote. I think that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. And I would like to let you know that before any military observer or military officers who form the battalions to work for the UN leave their countries, it's the normal practice that they are taught issues to do with the country they're going to; the historical background of the conflict, the -- the ethnic groups who are in that area; their differences, if any; the socio- cultural and other economic issues; and also the political situation in that particular area. So in this case there was no exception, and we were taught that in Nairobi before going to our area of responsibility. Secondly, as we arrived in Zagreb, we were briefed by the UNPROFOR officers on where we were going to be taken to, that is, where we would be posted, and the situation in those particular areas. We were also briefed on the historical background of the war itself, from when it started and even going back much, much earlier, into -- during the reign of the late Josip Broz Tito, coming all the way up to the Cold War period, and heading towards the period after the death of Josip Broz Tito and immediately thereafter, how the governments were formed and all that. So all that information we had. And every time you are taken to a different sector, you are also reminded about what is inherent in that particular sector. Like, my first posting was in Sector East, that was in Erdut. That is where I got posted for the first six months. And I was briefed about that particular area and the situation, because different areas had different problems. The issues which were inherent in Erdut and the surrounding areas, all the way up to Vukovar, are different from what we had in the Bosnian side. So upon my finishing the -- my stay in Team Erdut, I was given a proper brief. First of all, we had to get a break of about six days, and then you are briefed on your next posting and the area you are going to, and what is inherent in that particular area. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you all know, the situation was very different from how it was in Croatia which was slightly more peaceful, also very different from what was happening in Slovenia which was actually a bit independent at that time, and also different from what was happening in Macedonia. So we were briefed fully on what was happening in those areas. Maybe the last point on that particular section I can say, we were also briefed on the weaponry systems, or the weaponry systems which were used and available in those areas were shown to us through video and also pictures. And we were also taught how to identify those particular weapons when we see them, because some of them had been put in safe areas, that is, in some factories, to ensure that the warring factions do not access these weapons. This used to happen in areas where we could call safe areas, were called safe areas or enclaves, whatever name you may want to use. These are areas which were protected, or UNPA, UN Protected Areas, like Srebrenica, Zepa, and I think Sarajevo, and some other areas. Those were UN protected areas. So where -- these are areas where all the heavy weapons were put in particular places and we had to go and inspect them to make sure they had not gotten out. In any case one of the weapons is seen outside, we could easily identify because we had already been taught about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not want to interrupt you. I wanted to allow you to say everything you want. My next question is this: Who was it who briefed you when you were transferred from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Who was it? That's my first question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: We were briefed by the staff officers in the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb. Those are the ones who briefed us, the staff officers. These were serving under the Chief of Staff. But it was a regular brief, it was normal, and we got it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is that perhaps a convenient time for our second break? Thank you. Sir, we must have our next break now, and we will resume in half an hour at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue your cross-examination, Mr. Tolimir, I have to come back to some exhibits. We had a discussion among the Judges about one decision I made, and that is related to the documents P984 through P991. These were not used with this witness and not admitted during the Popovic case with this witness, and, therefore, I would like to ask the Defence if they object to admission of these documents we have already received, but otherwise normally we would only mark them for identification and admit them only if the -- there is a showing that there is a relation between these documents and the accused. But if there's no objection by the Defence, we would leave it like it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence does not have any objections to the admission of those documents and for the Prosecutor to express his opinion on what has just been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we leave it like it is, and these documents are exhibits with the given numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to leave no doubt on the record, these documents were, in fact, used with the witness. They just weren't admitted -- the LiveNote indicates that they were not used and not tendered but they were used and admitted through another witness. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They were not used in our trial with this witness but used in the other trial and admitted with another witness. I hope now it's clear for the record. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I did not interrupt you while you were talking about Western Slavonia and Erdut, and you also mentioned Vukovar and so on and so forth. Could you now tell us whether you discharged the same duties there. Did you appear in the role as a military observer and what was your role there, actually? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was a military observer in both Team Erdut and also in Team Srebrenica. In Erdut, I was the team leader, and when I went to Srebrenica, I joined as any other UNMO. The -- the roles and responsibilities of UN Military Observers are many. Some of them being to observe any violations to the cease-fire agreement and report on the same, to ensure that the -- the warring factions are brought together to a negotiation table so that they can discuss the problems they have. And in these, I'm talking about holding meetings with either side and conveying the grievances or feelings of one side to the other so that we can bridge the gap between the two factions. The other one was to ensure that the weapons which have been surrendered in a safe area, or UNPA, are kept in that safe area and no access to them by the faction that actually surrendered them. Another role was to negotiate for permission to leave or even enter the enclave on behalf of other UN agencies and NGOs. Some organisations, like UNHCR, IOM and all that, could not get access sometimes unless there is an intervention by the UN Military Observers. Also escort, give escort to some of these organisations so that they're not harmed on the way. One thing to note here is that military observers were never armed and even the current officers who are serving as military observers are not armed at all. Reason being, they should be in a position to access both sides without fear, without the other side fearing them, or them fearing the other side. If you're not armed, the other side will not fear you because can you cause no harm to them. So you can easily access their side. You can patrol the area without fear, because the only weapon that you have as a military observer is a pen and a book. That's -- those are the only weapons that you have. And also communication equipment. So really, those were the roles that we performed as military observers, and I did the same roles in both Team Erdut in Eastern Slavonia and also in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. When we're talking about that zone which is part of Croatia and the former Republic of Serbian Krajina and when it was demilitarised, were they -- were there volunteers who moved from that zone and joined the warfare in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I really do not understand which volunteers you are talking about, unless maybe you explain further. Are they volunteers to assist in terms of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A lot of soldiers were disarmed in that zone in both Eastern and Western Slavonia. I'm sure that are you familiar with the terms. Would you say that some of those men that had been disarmed as soldiers in those two areas, did they, later on, turn up in Bosnia and Herzegovina to engage in combat there? Did you hear of any such instances? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not hear of any instances whereby disarmed members or people from Eastern or Western Slavonia crossed over to Bosnia to fight. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that zone, was there a group known under the name of Skorpions? Does the name ring any bells? Thank you. People who called themselves Skorpions, a group of people.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember such a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember -- when you were in Srebrenica, do you remember how far Trnovo is from Srebrenica? Do you know where Trnovo is and how far it is from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is written alternative -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat the name of the place. Trnovo, T-r-n-o-v-o. That's the name of the place which was not properly recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I can't remember how far it was. It's a long time. But if I'm shown on the map I can easily identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it close to Srebrenica or was it in the zone that you controlled? Did you hear of as a geographic term?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Trnovo, unless the spelling mistake, really, I can't remember knowing such a place. But also there were so many places in that area that I may not remember. So that's why I was requesting if you show me on the map, I can easily identify whether it was in our area of responsibility or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That wasn't in your zone. I asked you whether you remember, and you don't, and I understand why, because the place is near Sarajevo. We don't need to look at a map. A crime had taken place in that place, committed by the alleged Skorpions. And the Skorpion group was composed of the people from the area where you had served in Western and Eastern Slavonia. They called themselves Skorpions. They came to this place Trnovo and committed a crime there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the people or the observers who can be able explain that are those who were serving in that particular area, because there must have been a team in that area. So if you ask me something to do with Srebrenica, or Team Erdut, I may be able to explain. But that was an area of responsibility of another team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted you to confirm that it did not feature in your reports, that you did not report about that crime, and that it did not belong to the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica where you served as an observer. Yes or no? Do you remember reporting about a crime committed by a group called Skorpions, originating from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never reported on anything from Western Slavonia, at all, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question. Why were you transferred from Eastern Slavonia to serve as a military observer in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the normal rotation of UN military observers is six months you stay in one team, and then another six months, you're transferred to another team. That was the normal rotation. But in case other conditions arose, maybe you are appointed team leader or deputy team leader in another team, you just transferred. So that was the normal UN system. But, at the same time it is good to note that I stayed there for only six months, which is normal, a normal rotation. So after six months I had to be transferred to another team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with this area of Western Slavonia that was under the control of the United Nations after you left? And Eastern Slavonia as well.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I know Eastern Slavonia was taken by the Croats. And Western Slavonia was also taken by the -- by the Croats. I am aware of that. I was there, I was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon arriving at Srebrenica, were you aware that, apart from being a protected area, it was also a demilitarised area, according to the agreement on safe areas signed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it then part of your mission to make sure that this area was demilitarised in keeping with the agreement and to check whether there were any violations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was our role to make sure that there are no violations to the cease-fire agreement. And that is why we had to ensure that all the weapons which had been surrendered to the -- to the UN. And in this particular case, that is, the Srebrenica issue, it was -- they were being kept at the Bravo Company of the DutchBat. That is near our PTT building, not very far from our PTT building. So that is where they were kept. And the -- the DutchBat are the ones who were to ensure that they're safe in that area and no one is allowed to take them from there. So that is all we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you supposed to note the presence of any armed persons within the borders of the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember whether, in your daily situation reports, there were any reports concerning the presence of armed persons in the demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is a time we noted some -- some -- some -- some men who were armed with small arms and we put that in our report, and it is here somewhere with us, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, as observers, receive information in any other way except by personal observation? Did you receive information from civilians or from the UNPROFOR, and did you pass on such information to your command? If so, please describe how.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received information from all sources. We had to make sure that we receive everything that is available to us. And not only what we see ourselves as military observers. So, in the process, when you are told something and you have not confirmed, you've got to indicate that it is not confirmed by you. So even in the situation reports that we used to send, something that comes as a rumour, hearsay, or whatever you may call it, we could put there NCBU, not confirmed by UNMOs. Secondly, we used to hold meetings with both factions and we could be told by this faction about the other and we could convey the same to the other, in terms of trying to ensure that no open hostilities arise, trying to ensure that the place remains safe, and also trying to make sure that these people are getting closer and closer to each other. But, at the same time, we had to communicate the same that we have received from those meetings to our higher echelons so that they know what is going on there. Some issues that -- that we conveyed to our higher echelons, that is, the UNMO headquarters, was -- you know, were meant to be discussed at other levels, not at our level. But we had to inform them what is happening so that they can be aware so that they can be able to investigate, and in case they want us to further investigate from the ground, they would tell us to do the same. And if you check most of the sitreps that are here, you will see something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer, you refer to some of the things that you mentioned in your statement on page 2. For the record, I would like the Registry to show you your statement in e-court, and that's Exhibit P992. I will be interested in paragraph 2, line 8, where you speak about your mission and what it consisted of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first page. Can we put it on the left side, with the English version on the right, and display the second page, second paragraph, line 8 of the statement in Serbian. In English, it's on page 3 -- or, rather, the next page. That is the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say in line 8 of the second paragraph, which is in fact the third one, you say: "The mission of the UNMO was mainly to observe and register violations of the demilitarisation agreement and bring the sides together and try to get them to come to a solution."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot find the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is perhaps on the next page but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's actually, I think, the prior page, page 2 of the English. Yes, top paragraph, I think: "The mission of the UNMO team was mainly to observe ..." Is that what General Tolimir was just reading? I think that is what General Tolimir was reading from is that top portion there, where it says: "The mission of the UNMO team ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's line 1 of the second paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see now what I've been reading? Do you remember your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From what I've just read, do I understand correctly that your main task was to observe violations of the demilitarisation agreement, as you indicated in this passage?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not written the main mission, as you're putting it. It's the mission and is just one of the roles, because even later on you can see I've said we also served as an intermediary between the factions. And even below there you can see I have written we reported activities to, you know, and all that. So it's not the main mission, as you've put it. It's one of the missions. Because, after all, if I may continue, after all, it was not in all areas in the former Yugoslavia where we had safe areas, not everywhere was a UN protected area. Not everywhere. The UN protected areas were just a few of them, I think there were five, that was Srebrenica, Zepa, Sarajevo, Bihac, and I think one other, to make five. Those were the only UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. However, if an area has the status of a demilitarised area and this status is violated, does that change the entire status of the area? Does it change your mission? And isn't it your primary task to make sure that the area remains demilitarised, in order to keep its status?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I really cannot be able to get what are you saying, because it's not us to demilitarise. It's not for the UN military observers to demilitarise an area. I explained much earlier that we were unarmed. The weapons we had were just a pen and a book. So our mission was not to demilitarise an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not suggest that it was your task to demilitarise. I suggested that your task was to observe whether the area was demilitarised or not and to report. You could only send reports but you could write in your report whether an area remained demilitarised or not. Let me ask you this: Was Tuzla a demilitarised area? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Demilitarised, I don't understand what you mean. But if you're talking about a UN protected area, Tuzla was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So Tuzla was just a protected area but not demilitarised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: What I mean is, a UN protected area had several designations. I don't know whether you can call designations, but the -- the protected area had to be demilitarised. So if Tuzla was not -- not a UN protected area, it didn't have to be demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that Tuzla, Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Sarajevo were all UN protected areas, under a UN resolution. Whereas, for instance, Tuzla held a US -- sorry, a NATO military base called Eagle. How was it then possible for Tuzla to be a protected area? Do you see the difference between -- is there a distinction, in fact, between protected and demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, for sure. Let me repeat that I did not mention Tuzla. When I was talking about the UN protected areas there is nowhere that I mentioned Tuzla, and you can go back to the report here. I never mentioned Tuzla at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can repeat those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Unless General Tolimir has some other source for this statement he has made, if we look at the LiveNote transcript at page 79, lines 7 and 8, Colonel Kingori specifically mentioned Srebrenica, Zepa, Sarajevo and Bihac. He never mentioned Tuzla as being a safe area and he's made it clear in his answer how he viewed Tuzla. So unless General Tolimir has another source for the basis of his question that suggests that Colonel Kingori said Tuzla was a safe area, then I think, at the very least, we're speaking at cross purposes, because no such thing was said today in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't say the witness said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am asking him, did Srebrenica have the same status as Tuzla? And is there a great difference between a protected area and a demilitarised area. Let's take Bihac, for example. Was Bihac a demilitarised area or not? Was it both demilitarised and protected?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: For the record, let me say straight and maybe a second time that Srebrenica was a UN protected area. Tuzla was not. So I don't know what else you want me to -- to say about -- they're two areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you perhaps clarify one point to avoid further discussions on that. What is the difference between a protected area and a demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A protected -- a UN protected area, sir, meant that the UN comes in there. The United Nations peacekeepers go in there to ensure that the people who are in there are safe, because they cannot be able to defend themselves. And in the process, an agreement has to be crafted to make sure that all the weapons held by these people who are inside there, the ones who were fighting there before, are kept in a safe place, and especially all the heavy weapons is -- this was mainly because of the Dayton Accord. It was agreed that all the weapons, all the heavy weapons have to be put in a safe area. And that is why the UN now came in as a maybe a battalion or two, depending on the size of the enclave to make sure that there is no attack that can be carried out from outside to the people living therein. So that is the demilitarisation bit and the protection. So you get demilitarised, then you get UN protection. On the other hand, the other parts of former Yugoslavia were just like that. People could fight, but, of course, in some areas, like if I give an example of Erdut area, that is that the Eastern Slavonia, though they had their own small arms, all the heavy weapons were put in various designated areas where we, as military observers could go there and check the weapons using a list that we had to ensure that no weapon has been taken away from that -- that area. But, at the same time, is good to know that they -- that is now -- if there is Eastern Slavonia, it's Croats themselves are the ones who are making sure that that the weapons are there. At times, we could go and find some of the weapons had been taken out. Or we could get reports that some of the weapons have been used against the other people. And so we could go there and investigate which is this type of weapon, from which store was -- was it taken out from, and then make our reports. And our reports were very strong in that now it would be dealt with at a higher level, to make sure that all those weapons are returned to the safe area. Safe area in this sense what I'm talking about is the store. So that they are not used against the other people at any other time. If we go back to Srebrenica itself, all the heavy weapons were removed from the Muslims and they were taken to Bravo Company. That is B Company of DutchBat. That compound, that is where those weapons were kept. And they were not removed from there at all. So that is why Srebrenica remained a UN protected area and also a demilitarised area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what is the difference between a protected area and demilitarised area and is there any difference to the status of that zone? In a protected area, did even small arms have to be removed and stored; whereas in a demilitarised area, both heavy weapons and other weapons had to be removed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness just has explained that. It was exactly the same question I put to the witness. But if there's any additional information you need, then carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But the witness did not explain the difference between Zepa and Slavonia. In Slavonia, only the heavy weapons were removed. The -- the light weapons were kept by the soldiers; whereas, in Srebrenica, both heavy weapons and light weapons were supposed to be removed, taken away from armed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Here we are talking about the -- the weapons being taken away from the Muslims in Srebrenica. And the heavy weapons, I just said, were kept in DutchBat, B Company. For the weapons that you're calling light weapons, they were also supposed to be taken away from them. And in fact they did not have those -- those weapons. But then, small arms, it was very difficult to control, you know, small arms. It is very difficult. Small arms, we're talking about like an AK 47, like pistols. Those are difficult to control in any situation, in any condition, and especially so during war it's very difficult to control, you know, small arms. But small arms cause minimal damage, and unlike the heavy weapons that the Bosnian Serbs had, they cannot cause a lot of harm. Contrary to maybe the line of thinking that we may take what there is, the Bosnian Serbs had all the weapons. They had the heavy weapons, they had the tanks, they had the artillery, the heavy pieces. We're talking about 155-millimetres howitzers. We are talking about mortars. We're talking about all those heavy weapons, even rockets. So these there's a difference between these two, if you compare the small arms, that is the AK 47 and pistols that maybe were left with the Muslims in the enclave and the heavy weapons surrounding them, really you cannot compare, really you cannot, because the Serbs were heavily armed and were not hiding it because with them, you know, that was normal. But those inside the enclave, the Muslims, all the heavy weapons, the mortars and all that, as I said earlier, were kept somewhere. But with small arms you could not be able to monitor all that. But compare the weaponry system of both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, we have reached the time for the break today. We have to continue the examination tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom. And, sir, please don't contact either party about the content of your testimony during the break. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow at 9.00.
